title: Roadmap Status Board
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: MicroSims Roadmap
Evidence Labels
Learning Analytics
Research Planning
description: A p5.js board of fourteen cards from Chapter 26 in two lanes: the five near-term roadmap items, each traced to a written source, and the five long-term ideas plus four open problem areas, each marked no source: speculative. Card color and a printed word show whether an item is built, designed or hoped for; clicking a card shows its source, the test that would show it worked and its main failure mode, and a quiz asks learners to label five cards.
audience: Teachers, instructional designers, learning-technology developers and learning-analytics practitioners (college undergraduate and professional development)

educational.topic: Separating built, designed and hoped-for claims on a roadmap
learningObjectives: The learner will distinguish what is built, designed and hoped for among the near-term and long-term items by opening each item and reading its source and its test.
prerequisites: The xAPI runtime and the Full LRS design (Chapters 17 and 20)

accessibility.notes: Labels are printed on cards and hoped-for cards have a dashed border, so color is not the only cue; the board is a Tab stop with arrow-key selection and B/D/H quiz keys; filter checkboxes and quiz buttons are native controls; describe() lists every visible card and its label; quiz progress is announced in an aria-live region

controls.label: Roadmap cards
controls.purpose: Open a card's label, source, required test and failure mode

controls.label: Built / Designed / Hoped for
controls.purpose: Show only cards with the checked labels

controls.label: Quiz me
controls.purpose: Hide labels and ask the learner to label five random cards

simulation.model: Static data set of fourteen roadmap cards with a labeling quiz
assumptions: Items the chapter calls partly built are shown as Built (verified adapters, shared sim libraries) or Designed (end-to-end POST path) with a partly built note
Every long-term idea and open problem is labeled hoped for, as the chapter states for the long-term half
No dates are given; the near-term horizon is about one year

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Clickable cards with a detail panel, filters and a labeling quiz
keyQuestions: What source does this item trace to?
What test would show it worked, and has it run?
Why can no long-term item be labeled built or designed yet?
commonMisconceptions: A written design means the feature exists
A partly built item is finished
An attractive long-term idea is supported by evidence
assessmentOpportunities: Rewriting a required test as a concrete study
Arguing for a label change with the chapter's definitions
